chief_complaints.text: I've been feeling tired all the time
My ankles and feet are swollen
My doctor said my kidney numbers were off on my blood test
I'm up all night going to the bathroom
I just don't have much of an appetite lately
I get short of breath just walking to the mailbox

hpi.onset: Gradual and silent; usually found on routine labs or when a complication appears
hpi.duration: Kidney damage present for more than 3 months by definition; symptoms often develop over months to years
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; many patients have no symptoms until kidney function is well below half of normal, and symptoms worsen as function declines further
hpi.location: Generalized; swelling in the legs, ankles, and around the eyes
hpi.quality: Vague tiredness, puffiness, poor appetite, and itching rather than a discrete pain
hpi.severity: Mild at first; can become disabling in advanced disease
hpi.timing: Fatigue worse through the day; nocturia most nights; itching worse at night

criteria.name: CKD definition and staging
criteria.summary: CKD is present when there is evidence of kidney damage (such as albuminuria, urine sediment abnormalities, or structural changes) or an eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for at least 3 months. Stages are based on eGFR: G1 ≥90, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 <15 mL/min/1.73 m². Albuminuria categories are A1 <30 mg/g, A2 30–300 mg/g, A3 >300 mg/g.

differential.name: Acute kidney injury
differential.why_considered: Rising creatinine and reduced urine output look identical on a single set of labs
differential.trigger: Creatinine that has risen over days to weeks rather than months to years, or a clear precipitant such as dehydration, contrast, or a new nephrotoxic drug

history: Recent vomiting, diarrhea, poor intake, or bleeding
New NSAID, contrast dye, or other nephrotoxic exposure
exam: Signs of volume depletion such as dry mucous membranes, low jugular venous pressure, or orthostatic changes
Normal or large kidneys rather than small ones
labs: Creatinine rising quickly between two draws
Fractional excretion of sodium or urea can help separate prerenal from intrinsic causes
FeNa below 1% suggests a prerenal picture
Muddy brown granular casts suggest acute tubular necrosis
imaging: Renal ultrasound shows normal-sized or enlarged kidneys without cortical thinning

differential.name: Nephrotic syndrome
differential.why_considered: Heavy proteinuria, low albumin, and edema overlap with advanced CKD
differential.trigger: Foamy urine with marked proteinuria, low serum albumin, and periorbital or generalized edema out of proportion to the creatinine

history: Abrupt or subacute onset of swelling
History of a systemic disease such as lupus or diabetes
exam: Normal or only mildly elevated blood pressure
labs: Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio in the nephrotic range
Serum albumin markedly low
Creatinine may be normal or only mildly elevated
Lipid panel often shows high cholesterol
imaging: Renal ultrasound may show normal or enlarged kidneys

differential.name: Heart failure
differential.why_considered: Fatigue, leg swelling, and shortness of breath are shared with CKD, and the two often coexist
differential.trigger: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or an S3 gallop with elevated jugular venous pressure

history: Waking at night short of breath
Known coronary disease or prior myocardial infarction
labs: Elevated BNP or NT-proBNP
Creatinine may be normal or only mildly elevated
imaging: Echocardiogram shows reduced ejection fraction or diastolic dysfunction
Chest x-ray shows pulmonary congestion or cardiomegaly

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Fatigue, cold intolerance, edema, and constipation overlap with CKD

exam: Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4
Creatinine usually normal or only mildly elevated

differential.name: Anemia of chronic disease
differential.why_considered: Normocytic anemia and fatigue are shared with CKD

history: Underlying inflammatory condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or chronic infection
Nocturia and foamy urine are absent
labs: Low hemoglobin with normal creatinine and eGFR
Low iron with low transferrin saturation but normal or high ferritin
Urinalysis without protein or blood

differential.name: Multiple myeloma
differential.why_considered: Anemia, fatigue, and elevated creatinine from light chain kidney injury can mimic CKD
differential.trigger: Anemia with bone pain, hypercalcemia, or a high total protein with a low albumin gap

history: Bone pain, especially back or ribs
labs: Elevated total protein with low albumin
Hypercalcemia
Proteinuria that is not primarily albumin on urine protein electrophoresis
Serum free light chain ratio abnormal
imaging: Skeletal survey or whole-body low-dose CT shows lytic lesions

differential.name: Renal artery stenosis
differential.why_considered: Progressive kidney dysfunction with difficult-to-control hypertension

history: Resistant hypertension on three or more agents
Onset of hypertension after age 55 or before age 30
exam: Abdominal bruit over the epigastrium or flank
labs: Creatinine rises after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
Hypokalemia from secondary hyperaldosteronism
imaging: Magnetic resonance angiography or CT angiography shows narrowing at the origin of a renal artery

differential.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
differential.why_considered: Fatigue and shortness of breath are shared, and both are common in older smokers

labs: Normal creatinine and eGFR
Elevated bicarbonate from chronic CO2 retention
imaging: Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms

severity.mild: CKD stage G1–G2 with albuminuria or G3a: eGFR 45–89 mL/min/1.73 m², no symptoms, normal or near-normal exam, detected on routine labs
severity.moderate: CKD stage G3b: eGFR 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m², mild fatigue, early anemia, rising phosphate and PTH, mild leg edema, hypertension
severity.severe: CKD stage G4: eGFR 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m², marked fatigue, anemia, edema, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, itching, restless legs, early uremic symptoms
severity.critical: CKD stage G5 (kidney failure): eGFR below 15 mL/min/1.73 m², uremic symptoms with nausea, vomiting, confusion, asterixis, pericarditis, pulmonary edema, severe hyperkalemia, or refractory acidosis; dialysis or transplant needed

special_populations.differences: Creatinine may look normal despite reduced kidney function because of low muscle mass; use eGFR and cystatin C when available. Symptoms are often attributed to aging, and polypharmacy raises the risk of drug accumulation and nephrotoxicity.

Diabetes is the most common cause of CKD in the US. Albuminuria often appears before eGFR falls. Tight glucose control and ACE inhibitors or ARBs slow progression. Metformin dose must be adjusted and stopped when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².

Preeclampsia can mimic or worsen CKD with hypertension, proteinuria, and edema. Creatinine normally falls in pregnancy, so a value in the normal nonpregnant range may indicate kidney dysfunction. CKD raises the risk of preterm delivery and fetal growth restriction.

CKD in children is usually caused by congenital anomalies or inherited disease rather than diabetes or hypertension. Growth failure and delayed puberty are key concerns, and dosing of all medications must be weight-based.

Patients already on dialysis may have minimal urine output and depend on the machine for fluid and electrolyte balance. Missed dialysis sessions cause rapid volume overload, hyperkalemia, and uremic symptoms.

Obesity increases the risk of CKD and can make blood pressure and edema assessment harder. Weight loss and GLP-1 receptor agonists may slow progression, but dosing and volume status need careful monitoring.

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any change in how much you urinate, or are you waking up at night to urinate?
key_questions.looking_for: Nocturia and gradual decline in urine output suggest chronic kidney dysfunction rather than an acute process

key_questions.question: How long have you been feeling tired or noticed swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms present for months to years, supporting chronicity rather than acute kidney injury

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any foamy or bubbly urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Foamy urine suggests proteinuria, a marker of kidney damage

key_questions.question: Have you had any blood tests showing kidney problems before this visit?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior elevated creatinine or reduced eGFR documented more than 3 months ago confirms chronicity

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes or high blood pressure?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes and hypertension are the most common causes of CKD in the US

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a kidney injury, kidney stones, or urinary blockage?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior AKI, stones, or obstruction increase risk of CKD

key_questions.question: Do you take any pain relievers like ibuprofen or naproxen regularly?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic NSAID use is nephrotoxic and can worsen kidney function

key_questions.question: Are you taking any blood pressure medicines, diabetes medicines, or water pills?
key_questions.looking_for: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, and metformin require dose adjustment in CKD

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had kidney failure or needed dialysis?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of kidney failure or polycystic kidney disease raises suspicion for inherited causes

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any itching, poor appetite, nausea, or muscle cramps?
key_questions.looking_for: Uremic symptoms suggest more advanced CKD

key_questions.question: Have you had any chest pain, shortness of breath when lying flat, or swelling in your legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Volume overload or pericarditis, which can complicate advanced CKD

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have anemia or low blood count?
key_questions.looking_for: Anemia of CKD from low erythropoietin is common

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or drink alcohol?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking and alcohol use affect cardiovascular risk and CKD progression

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, burning with urination, or blood in your urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Absence of these argues against acute infection or glomerulonephritis; presence may indicate a different or superimposed process

reasoning_points: Kidney damage or reduced eGFR persisting for more than 3 months defines chronicity
eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² or markers of kidney damage such as albuminuria, urine sediment abnormalities, or structural changes
Diabetes and hypertension are the most common causes in US adults
Symptoms are often absent until kidney function is significantly reduced; fatigue, edema, nocturia, and itching are common late findings
Laboratory findings include elevated creatinine, anemia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperphosphatemia, and low albumin
Urinalysis may show proteinuria, hematuria, or casts depending on the underlying cause
Renal ultrasound typically shows small, echogenic kidneys with cortical thinning
Staging uses eGFR categories G1–G5 and albuminuria categories A1–A3 to guide management and referral
Reversible causes such as obstruction, nephrotoxic drugs, and volume depletion must be excluded before labeling as CKD
Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in CKD; blood pressure and glucose control slow progression
